claims.text: A dual-channel framework will predict HfNbTaTiZr thermal conductivity more accurately than earlier methods.
Below 200 K, lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions in HfNbTaTiZr are of similar magnitude.
HfNbTaTiZr containing approximately 1 wt.% oxygen has a total thermal conductivity of 10–17 W/(K m) from 300 to 1200 K.
The proposed framework will achieve prediction errors of approximately ±20%.
An error of approximately ±20% represents about a 30% improvement over previous estimates.
The modeled initial states are single-phase, defect-free HfNbTaTiZr crystals, either undoped or containing approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
The proposed framework computes lattice transport using machine-learned, on-the-fly force fields.
The proposed framework estimates electronic transport separately using ab initio electronic structures and temperature-dependent scattering rates.
Machine-learned force fields will capture anharmonicity and local lattice distortions relevant to lattice heat transport.
Chemical disorder produces local lattice distortion and force-constant fluctuations that affect phonon scattering.
Oxygen impurities induce local lattice distortions and force-constant fluctuations in HfNbTaTiZr.
Chemical disorder affects phonon and electronic heat transport through distinct scattering responses.
Separately simulating phonon and electronic scattering avoids oversimplifications associated with using a single Debye temperature.
Earlier methods typically conflate lattice and electronic transport and therefore fail to capture the distinct scattering mechanisms in HfNbTaTiZr.
The framework is applicable below 200 K and from 300 to 1200 K for single-phase, chemically homogeneous specimens with low-level oxygen.
Accuracy may degrade in heavily defected or multiphase specimens.
Below approximately 50 K, additional omitted scattering mechanisms may dominate.
Model accuracy depends on force-field calibration and on the fidelity of the ab initio electronic-scattering estimates.
Independent low-temperature measurements of lattice and electronic contributions can decisively test the predicted comparability below 200 K.
High-temperature total-conductivity measurements and an error comparison against earlier methods can falsify the claimed 10–17 W/(K m), ±20%, and 30% improvement targets.

contradictions.description: The initial state calls oxygen-containing crystals defect-free, while other fields treat oxygen as an impurity that creates local distortions and distinguish such sources from an ideal defect-free state.
The conditions state applicability generally below 200 K, but the boundary says accuracy may degrade below approximately 50 K; the validated lower-temperature limit is therefore internally ambiguous.
